This is a common practice in EMS. Certain people are marked for "two car responses," meaning that if there is a call at their house, there need to be at least two officers before going in. This is typically for angry, violent people. The ambulance waits down the street until the scene is safe. Cases like an old person that has an angry son that doesn't want them treated, but they are unconscious and dying.

That may not scale well to a mass murder situation. The people being hurt are not connected to the person making it dangerous. Most importantly, time is a critical factor in reducing casualties. Generally, the scene is called "hot" when it is unsafe, and "cold" when it is safe. Applying this to the incident as a whole is safest for EMS, meaning there is low risk of the shooter getting to them because the whole place has been cleared.

So instead, the school is divided into zones. Areas that have not been checked are hot, and areas that are confirmed safe are considered cold. EMS are not allowed into hot zones. As more of the school is cleared, the cold zone expands, and the medics move up. Some places now let them into "warm" zones, where they push forward with the police, but just behind them with another cop for protection. I think that is quite rare because it requires a lot of interagency cooperation which is not often practiced. Communications are also an issue, for example using radios within the building is difficult because of the thick concrete walls. In addition, my county's police/fire/ems radios have only been interoperable for about a year. Before the multi-million dollar program for a rural county, you had to have two seperate radios. This is not uncommon, and was one of the problems cited in the aftermath of 9/11.

TL;DR Scene safety is the number one rule, and without practice the system may not be ideal. There are definitely reasons to wait before entering a hot scene. If the incident commander won't allow them in, that's pretty much the end of it.
